title: Public Wi-Fi, and what a VPN really does
body_md:
## Two networks, almost one name

Your laptop finds two networks in the café: Daily_Grind and Daily_Grind_Guest. One belongs to the café. The other could belong to anyone with a phone and a free hour, and nothing on the screen says which is which.

That is the difficulty with a public network: somebody else runs it. A lookalike name or a sign-in page (a captive portal) can walk you into a fake login, and a hostile network can see a little about your connections (who you contact, and when) and tamper with anything unencrypted. Most of the web, though, now uses HTTPS, which keeps a page’s contents private even on a stranger’s Wi-Fi, and the FTC says public Wi-Fi is usually safe when the sites you use are encrypted.

Read the padlock for exactly what it says: your connection to the domain in the address bar is encrypted. It does not say the page belongs to your bank, and a phishing site can hold a valid certificate too.

### Before you join

When you can, check the network name (the SSID) with staff or an official sign. Turn off auto-join for networks you don’t know. A sign-in page may fairly ask you to accept terms or type a room number, but an email password, a bank code or permission to install software is a reason to leave. And never click through a certificate warning.

If a task matters and something feels off, switch to mobile data or your own hotspot and open the service through its installed app or a saved address. Mobile data has risks of its own and vouches for no website; the aim is only to leave the questionable network.

## What a VPN does, and where it stops

Picture a VPN as a covered walkway from your device to the VPN company’s server. From the sidewalk, people see you step in and nothing of what happens inside, but only for traffic you actually send through it. That shrinks what the local network learns about you, and some employers require it for private work systems. It also moves some of your trust: the VPN operator now sees part of what the café would have seen.

The walkway has gaps. Split tunneling, apps excluded from the VPN, a dropped connection or a captive portal can all leave traffic outside it. Check the provider’s documentation and the app’s “connected” status; what a “kill switch” is called, and what it does, varies.

And the walkway comes out onto the ordinary street. Neither a VPN nor a hotspot fixes a fake destination, a stolen password, a malicious download or an infected device. Don’t buy one because a web page calls every public network a trap.

### On every network, the same habits

Keep your device updated, use two-step sign-in (MFA) and check where you are going. For a sensitive site on public Wi-Fi, type the address or use a saved one, read the whole domain, check for HTTPS and stop at any warning. If the network looks tampered with, put the task off. If you typed credentials into a suspicious sign-in page, disconnect, forget the network and, from a separate connection, change the password on every account you entered.

widget_config.goal: Pick a safe way to do something sensitive on public Wi-Fi, and say exactly which risks a VPN covers and which it leaves alone.
widget_config.today_action: Before your next stint on public Wi-Fi, turn off auto-join for unfamiliar networks, update your device, and save a direct route to your bank or another service that matters.
widget_config.scope: General advice for ordinary users, checked 2026-10-20. The people and places in the examples are invented. The FTC page is aimed at the US and dates from 2023; the NCSC document is about organizational VPNs and is used here only for how a tunnel works. Results depend on the network, the device and the VPN settings.

sources.title: FTC: Public Wi-Fi networks
sources.scope: US consumer guidance from February 2023: HTTPS, public Wi-Fi and fake sites.

sources.title: NCSC: Virtual private networks
sources.scope: UK guidance for organizations: how traffic is routed through a tunnel and where captive portals get in the way. Not an endorsement of any personal VPN.

blocks.title: The airport “security update”
blocks.situation: At the gate, Alex joins a network called Airport_Free. Before it will show a flight status, it wants a “security update” certificate installed and an email password typed in.
blocks.analysis: A network’s name proves nothing about who runs it, and installing a certificate changes what the device trusts. Alex asks airport staff for the real network name, refuses the install, and checks the flight on mobile data or in the airline’s own app. It was the demand for a password and a certificate that gave the game away. A sign-in page on its own would not have.

blocks.title: A hotel portal that wants a room number
blocks.situation: At check-in the clerk tells Jo the exact Wi-Fi name. The network’s page asks for a room number and a tick beside the terms, and then a news site Jo knows loads over HTTPS.
blocks.analysis: The name came from the clerk, not from the network itself, and what the page asks for is small and ordinary. Jo can browse as usual, still checks anything sensitive, and treats neither the portal nor a VPN as a guarantee. If the page ever asks for a bank code, she stops.

blocks.title: Choosing a connection at a station
blocks.setup: Four invented moments at a station. Each starts fresh, and what you chose before does not decide the next network. No real credentials or sites are touched.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 1. Two station networks have almost the same name. Which one do you join?

choices.consequence: The strongest signal in the hall might be a hotspot someone set up beside you.
choices.explanation: Signal strength tells you how close a transmitter is, not who runs it.

choices.text: Ask station staff, or find the official name on a sign, before joining.
choices.consequence: You are far less likely to land on a lookalike.
choices.explanation: A name that looks right is not proof of who runs the network.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 2. On another station network, the sign-in page says you must install a “security certificate” before you can go online.

choices.text: Install it and get online faster.
choices.consequence: Your device may start trusting whoever issued that certificate, on this connection and later ones.
choices.explanation: An installed certificate stays on your device after you leave the station, and it decides what the device will trust.

choices.text: Decline, and switch to mobile data or ask staff how to connect.
choices.consequence: No unknown certificate gets added to your device.
choices.explanation: Joining ordinary public Wi-Fi does not call for a new certificate on your device.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 3. On mobile data, you tap a link in a text message and land on a page that looks like your bank’s. The address bar shows HTTPS.

choices.text: Close it and open the bank’s app or a saved address.
choices.consequence: Your banking starts at a destination you already trust.
choices.explanation: Neither mobile data nor HTTPS vouches for a link that arrived in a message.

choices.text: Enter your details, since mobile data and HTTPS are both in place.
choices.consequence: The fake site still receives everything you type.
choices.explanation: An encrypted connection tells you nothing about who is on the other end.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 4. A colleague insists you can’t use the station Wi-Fi without a VPN. What do you say?

choices.text: Explain what the tunnel covers, and still check the destination and HTTPS.
choices.consequence: The VPN covers the road to its server, and your own checks cover the rest.
choices.explanation: A VPN protects the traffic it carries to its own server. It does nothing about a scam page at the other end.

choices.text: Buy the first VPN you see advertised and ignore the site’s warnings.
choices.consequence: The bad destination or the certificate problem is still there.
choices.explanation: A VPN is no substitute for checking.

blocks.debrief: Play it again and, at each step, say aloud who or what you are being asked to trust: the hotspot, your device’s certificate list, the website, the tunnel.

blocks.title: Carry it to the next network

questions.prompt: A new online shop has a valid HTTPS certificate. What does that establish?

choices.text: That your connection to its displayed domain is encrypted.
choices.explanation: It says nothing about whether the seller is honest.

questions.prompt: A VPN app shows “connected,” but it is set to carry only your work apps. What is covered?

choices.text: All the traffic from your device, automatically.
choices.explanation: A “connected” icon does not tell you which traffic goes through the tunnel.

choices.text: Only the traffic selected for the tunnel.
choices.explanation: With split or per-app settings, everything else travels outside it.

questions.prompt: Staff confirmed the hotel’s network name, and its portal asks for your room number. What fits?

choices.text: It may well be legitimate. Judge what it asks for, and treat your sensitive logins as a separate matter.
choices.explanation: Portals are often perfectly normal, but they vouch for none of the sites you visit afterwards.

choices.text: Treat every portal as an attack.
choices.explanation: That mistakes an ordinary sign-in routine for a scam.

questions.prompt: Your bank’s page throws a certificate warning. What do you do?

choices.text: Continue, since a VPN is on.
choices.explanation: A VPN does not repair a site’s certificate.

choices.text: Stop, and reach the bank by a known route or from another network.
choices.explanation: Do not override a failed identity check when sensitive data is at stake.
